parts.problem_md:
Study Figs. 1.2 and 1.3, which show information about birth rates in Vietnam (an MIC in South East Asia). ![q1b-specimen-2020-paper-1-cie-igcse-geo](assets/001-q1b-specimen-2020-paper-1-cie-igcse-geo.png) | The communist government of Vietnam is penalising couples who have more than two children. In the early 1960s it imposed a two-child limit for couples and there have been campaigns to promote contraception and abortion in the country since 1997.

By 2000, the birth rate had been reduced considerably by the use of fines and confiscation of land. The original policy ended in 2003 but was revived in 2008 after an increase in the birth rate.

Villagers in Thua Thien-Hue province are being fined for having more than two children under the government two-child policy. Catherine Pham Thi Thanh, 44, said that since 1996 she has been fined a total of 3800 kilograms of rice for having six children. This is a great loss for the family which makes an annual profit of only 700 kilograms of rice from their farm. | |---| Fig 1.3 Suggest how government policies and other factors may have reduced Vietnam's birth rate.
parts.solution_md:
Vietnam's government has imposed an anti-natalist policy which restricts the number of children people have.** [1]** To enforce this they have used fines if people do not follow the policy so people have had fewer children.** [d]** The government has also made contraception cheaper **[1]** and run campaigns encouraging people to use contraception which reduced the number of children people have. **[d]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word is '**suggest**' this means that the answer needs to give reasons for the ways the Vietnamese government's policies have affected birth rates.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - One mark for each simple point **[1]**
> - One mark for a developed point **[d]**
> 
> Answers can be either:
> 
> - Four simple points
> - One developed point plus two simple points
> - Two points which are developed
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - Education of women
> - Women focussing on careers
> - Later marriages
> - Improvement in healthcare
> - Reduction in infant mortality

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although there is some information in the sources the question also mentions other factors. This means that you can use your knowledge of anti-natalist policies to suggest other reasons that the birth rate may have fallen.

parts.problem_md:
Study Fig. 6.1, which shows information about population growth in The Gambia (an LEDC in Africa).

![Text discussing The Gambia's high population growth rate due to low contraceptive use, polygamy, and reduced infant mortality, with family planning efforts since 1993.](assets/002-text-discussing-the-gambia-s-high-population-gro.png)

*Fig 6.1*

Explain why it is difficult to reduce natural population growth rates in LICs, such as The Gambia, even though the use of contraception has recently increased.
parts.solution_md:
In The Gambia previously the infant mortality rate was high** [1]** this led people to have more children to ensure that some survived to adulthood which has continued even though infant mortality has decreased. **[d]** Women in The Gambia are less likely to be educated **[1]** and often marry at a young age** [1]**. This increases the number of children each women is likely to have. **[d]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word is '**explain**' this means that the answer needs to give reasons for the high birth rate in The Gambia.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - One mark for each simple point  **[1] **
> - One mark for a developed point **[d]**
> 
> Answers can be either:
> 
> - Five simple points
> - One developed point plus two simple points
> - Two points which are developed
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - Polygamy - men may have children with several wives
> - Reduction in death rates
> - Improvement in healthcare/medicines
> - Improved sanitation
> - Improved water supply
> - Better food supply
> - Cultural expectations for large families
> - Need for children to help with family or earning money
> - Lack of government anti-natal policy

parts.problem_md:
Study Fig 5.1, which shows the demographic transition model (DTM).

![Demographic transition model chart showing birth, death, and total population rates across five stages from high stationary to negative growth.](assets/003-demographic-transition-model-chart-showing-birth.png)

*The demographic transition model*

The UK is a HIC. Which stage of the demographic transition model is the UK?

**Extract:**

Study Fig 5.1, which shows the demographic transition model (DTM).

What are three population characteristics of a country at stage 2 of the demographic transition model?
parts.solution_md:
**High birth rates** **[1 mark]**

**Decreasing death rates ****[1 mark]**

**Increasing total population**** [1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Study Fig 5.1, which shows the demographic transition model (DTM).

State three reasons why the birth rate starts to fall rapidly in stage 3 of the model.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> Any** three** from:
> 
> - Increased birth control
> - Family planning
> - Increased cost of raising children
> - Low infant mortality rate
> - More access to education for women

parts.problem_md: Explain the strengths of the demographic transition model.
parts.solution_md:
The demographic transition model provides a clear framework for understanding population change over time.**[1]** For example, it shows how birth and death rates change as countries develop economically.**[d]** The model is useful for predicting future population trends**[1]** which helps governments plan for services like healthcare and education.**[d]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each simple point **[1]**
> - 1 mark for a developed point **[d]**
> 
> Answers can be either:
> 
> - 4 simple points
> - 1 developed point plus 2 simple points
> - 2 points which are developed
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - The model helps compare different countries at various stages of development
> - It identifies clear stages that most countries follow during demographic transition

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is explain, so say why each feature is a strength, not just what the model shows
> 
> Develop points for the extra marks, e.g. link a strength to a real consequence such as planning services

parts.problem_md: Explain the limitations of the demographic transition model.
parts.solution_md:
The demographic transition model does not take into account migration or government policies.** [1] **For example, China's one child policy which had a significant impact on population change. **[d]** The model is based on countries in Western Europe** [1]** which means it is harder to apply to MICs and LICs today. **[d]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each simple point  **[1] **
> - 1 mark for a developed point **[d]**
> 
> Answers can be either:
> 
> - 4 simple points
> - 1 developed point plus 2 simple points
> - 2 points which are developed
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of a response to this question. Other information that could be used in the answer includes:
> 
> - Industrialisation in MICs and LICs  is happening over a much shorter time
> - The model assumes all countries populations change in the same ways
> - The model does not account for declining or ageing populations in some countries today
> - The model cannot predict unexpected events such as pandemics/viruses

> **[exam-tip]**
> Within geography there are lots of models used to show trends or patterns. It is important to recognise that these models have limitations, and to know what some of these limitations are.

![Table displaying figures: births 14,270; deaths 15,670; immigration 13,030; emigration 6,940.](assets/005-table-displaying-figures-births-14-270-deaths-15.png)

How is natural population change calculated?

**Extract:**

Study Fig 3.1, which shows information about population change in Estonia (an HIC in Europe) in 2018.

Table displaying figures: births 14,270; deaths 15,670; immigration 13,030; emigration 6,940.

The total population of Estonia on 1 January 2018 was 1319130. Calculate the total population of Estonia by the end of 2018 using the statistics in Fig. 3.1. You should show your calculations.
parts.solution_md:
*(Births - deaths) 14 270 - 15 670 *= -1400

*(Immigration  - emigration) 13 030 - 6940* = 6090

*1 319 130 - 1400 + 6090* =** 1 323 820**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> - One mark **[1] **awarded for showing the calculation

> **[exam-tip]**
> All parts of the calculation must be shown to gain the mark for showing calculations.

parts.problem_md:
The one-child policy was a strategy used by the government of China to influence natural population growth rates.

Use Figure 2.2 to evaluate the impacts of the one-child policy on population growth in China.

![Graph showing birth and death rates per 1000 people in China from 1962 to 2020, highlighting the impact of the one-child policy starting in 1980.](assets/007-graph-showing-birth-and-death-rates-per-1000-peo.png)
parts.solution_md:
The birth rate in China decreased from 18 per 1000 to 12 per 1000 **[1] **showing that the policy overall was successful **[d]** however, the reduction was not immediate **[1]**. The birth rate decrease was faster in the 1960s and 1970s ** [1] **when it decreased from  43 per 1000 in 1963 to 18 per 1000 in 1980** [1].**
